title: The maintenance agent's first month
scenario:
You manage operations at a property company with 900 flats. A maintenance agent will handle repair requests from tenants: it reads the request, books a contractor, sends reminders and pays small invoices.

The team drafted an autonomy sheet using the course's four-step ladder (1 Suggest, 2 Ask first, 3 Act within limits, 4 Act and report). Go-live is next week. The exhibit shows the draft.
exhibit:
Maintenance agent: autonomy sheet, draft v1 (made-up example data)

Action                              Can undo?   Step   Track record
Sort requests by urgency             yes         3      400 test cases, 2 errors
Send appointment reminder SMS        partly      2      none yet
Book a contractor visit              yes         2      none yet
Pay contractor invoices up to €5,000 no          4      none yet
Cancel a tenant's booking            partly      3      none yet

Team note: "Prompts slow us down. Could we just run the whole
agent in a bypass mode, like the coding tools have?"

questions.prompt: Which line of the sheet is the most dangerous as drafted?

options.text: Sort requests by urgency at step 3, because sorting needs a person to check every case.
options.explanation: Sorting can be undone and has a test record (400 cases, 2 errors). Step 3 is a reasonable choice.

options.text: Book a contractor visit at step 2, because booking is too risky for an agent at all.
options.explanation: Step 2 means a person approves each booking. That is a careful start, not a danger.

options.text: Pay invoices up to €5,000 at step 4: a payment can't be undone and there is no record yet.
options.explanation: Right. A high cost of mistake, no undo and no evidence all point to a low step, such as 2 (Ask first).

options.text: Send reminder SMS at step 2, because reminders should never need any approval.
options.explanation: With no record yet, asking first is a safe start. The lesson's rule is to start low and move up with evidence.

questions.prompt: How should you answer the team note about a bypass mode?

options.text: Agree: one mode for the whole agent is simpler to manage than a step per action.
options.explanation: Simpler, but it gives the riskiest action (payments) the same freedom as sorting. The lesson sets a step per action.

options.text: Disagree: Claude Code's docs keep bypass mode for isolated containers and VMs only; set each action's step instead.
options.explanation: Right. In bypass mode everything runs without asking. The docs limit it to isolated environments, and this agent works with real money and real tenants.

options.text: Agree, if the agent's instructions say "never pay more than you should".
options.explanation: An instruction is not a limit. In bypass mode everything runs without a prompt, whatever the instruction says.

options.text: Disagree: bypass mode adds extra prompts, so it would slow the team down even more.
options.explanation: The opposite: in bypass mode everything runs without asking. That is exactly why the docs limit it to isolated environments.

questions.prompt: Three months later, reminder SMS has 1,200 approvals and 0 changes by staff. What fits the vendor guidance best?

options.text: Move reminders up one step, to step 3, and write down the evidence for the change.
options.explanation: Right. Anthropic's SDK docs suggest loosening permissions as trust builds, and OpenAI's MCP guide says you can skip approvals once you trust a server.

options.text: Move every action up one step, because the agent has now proved itself.
options.explanation: The record is for reminders only. Payments and cancellations have their own risks and their own records.

options.text: Keep reminders at step 2 forever, because an agent's step should never change.
options.explanation: Both vendors describe autonomy that grows with trust. Never moving up wastes staff time.

options.text: Move reminders straight to step 4 and stop checking them at all.
options.explanation: The lesson moves one step at a time. Step 4 also means working in a separated space, but SMS reach real tenants.

questions.prompt: A manager says: "Staff approve almost everything. Replace all approvals, payments included, with an automatic safety checker." What is the best reply?

options.text: Agree: if people approve almost everything, their approvals add no safety.
options.explanation: Fatigue is real, but a checker can miss things too. The answer is fewer, better prompts, not none on payments.

options.text: Agree, as long as the checker reads the agent's own reason for each payment before deciding.
options.explanation: Anthropic's auto mode post removes the agent's own messages from what its classifier sees, on purpose, so the agent can't talk the checker into a bad call.

options.text: Disagree: approvals must always stay on every action, even sorting.
options.explanation: Too many prompts cause approval fatigue. Low-risk actions with a good record can move up.

options.text: Partly: automate low-risk prompts, but keep a person on payments.
options.explanation: Right. Anthropic's auto mode post reports approval fatigue (93% of prompts approved), but its classifier missed 17% of real overeager actions and is not a replacement for careful human review on high-stakes infrastructure.
